pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: What exactly is `http.HandlerFunc`, and how is it different from `http.Handler`? When would you still write a struct handler like `versionHandler` instead of a plain function?
expected_points: http.Handler is the one-method interface: ServeHTTP(w, r) — everything (endpoints, mux, middleware, server) speaks it
http.HandlerFunc is a named function type with a ServeHTTP method that just calls the function — an adapter from an ordinary function to the interface, not a second kind of handler

a struct handler carries state with it (version string, logger, database handle); a closure can also capture dependencies, so the struct is a style choice for handlers with several fields or their own methods

questions.prompt: Walk me through the routes you registered. What does `GET /health` give you for free that you would otherwise hand-code, why is the home page `GET /{$}` and not `GET /`, and how does the handler read the name out of `GET /greet/{name}`?
expected_points: the method prefix means non-GET requests get 405 with a correct Allow header from the mux, no r.Method checks in handlers
a pattern ending in / is a subtree root, so "/" matches every path and unknown paths would never 404; {$} anchors the match to exactly "/"
{name} matches one path segment and r.PathValue("name") reads it
when several patterns match, the most specific wins regardless of registration order; irreconcilable conflicts panic at registration

questions.prompt: `Chain(mux, RequestID, Logging(logger), Recover)` — trace a request through it, and explain why your loop over the middleware slice runs backwards. What breaks if RequestID and Logging swap places?
expected_points: a middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler: a closure over next, adapted with HandlerFunc
execution nests like an onion: RequestID before, Logging before, Recover before, handler, then the after-halves in reverse order — the first listed is outermost and finishes last
wrapping backwards is what makes the first-listed middleware the outermost layer, since the middleware applied last ends up on the outside
with Logging outside RequestID the id is not on the context yet when the log line is written, so request_id comes out empty — nothing fails, the telemetry just gets worse

questions.prompt: Your logger needs the response status, but `http.ResponseWriter` has no way to read it back. How did you solve that, and why does `statusWriter` have to start at 200?
expected_points: embed http.ResponseWriter in a wrapper so it satisfies the interface for free, override WriteHeader to record the code before delegating, and pass the wrapper to next
a handler that only writes a body never calls WriteHeader — the server sends an implicit 200, so a zero-valued status field would log 0
a fresh wrapper per request, because handlers run concurrently on separate goroutines
bonus: the wrapper hides Flusher/Hijacker unless it offers Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter for http.NewResponseController

questions.prompt: `http.Server`'s timeouts all default to zero. What does zero mean, and what specific failure does each of ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout and IdleTimeout prevent?
expected_points: zero means wait forever — the default server has no defence at all

ReadTimeout caps reading the request (headers plus body): the defence against slow or deliberately dripping senders such as slowloris; ReadHeaderTimeout is the narrower version when uploads are legitimately slow
WriteTimeout caps producing and writing the response: bounds hung handlers and clients that read one byte at a time
IdleTimeout caps how long a keep-alive connection may sit between requests, so old clients cannot park sockets and exhaust file descriptors
they are whole-connection backstops, not per-request budgets — the per-request tool is the request context

questions.prompt: A deploy sends your process SIGTERM while three requests are in flight. Walk me from the signal to the process exit, and say why `http.ErrServerClosed` is not an error.
expected_points: signal.NotifyContext turns the signal into a cancelled context, so the rest of the program only deals with cancellation

Shutdown stops accepting new connections, closes idle ones, and waits for active requests up to the deadline of the context it is given — which must be a fresh context, not the one that was just cancelled
Serve unblocks with http.ErrServerClosed, which is the confirmation that shutdown happened; treating it as failure makes every clean deploy look like a crash
without this, in-flight requests die mid-response and users see errors on every restart

questions.prompt: Why does `Run` take a `net.Listener` instead of calling `srv.ListenAndServe()`? What does that buy the tests?
expected_points: separating listen from serve makes the server testable: tests bind 127.0.0.1:0, so the OS picks a free port and nothing collides or reaches the network
the caller decides where to listen (systemd socket, a pre-bound port, a fake) — the same dependency-injection instinct as passing a clock or an http.Client
the test can watch the exact listener it created, e.g. to check that shutdown really closed it

questions.prompt: The server runs every request on its own goroutine. What does that mean for state you put in a handler or middleware, and why do these exercises run under `go test -race`?
expected_points: any value shared across requests (a map, a counter, a cached struct) is touched concurrently and needs synchronization or immutability
per-request values must be created inside the handler function — e.g. the statusWriter — or requests will overwrite each other
request-scoped data travels on the request context, not in package-level variables
the race detector catches exactly the bugs that load testing hides and production finds
